title: Stand firm
hook: the good lies in the will, so stand firm there (Discourses 1.29)
carry: let the branches move in the wind

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sparring partner, the rough opponent a trainer chooses for you. Your line was what is this making of me. Today ends the week.

A tree in a storm doesn't stay still. The branches thrash, leaves tear off, the whole crown bends sideways. What keeps it standing is underneath, out of sight: the roots, gripping the ground. A tree that tried to hold every leaf in place would snap. Epictetus has a whole chapter on constancy, on staying steady when pressure comes, and his advice runs the same way as the tree's. Know where your roots are.
screen: `A TREE IN A STORM.` → `BRANCHES THRASH, ROOTS HOLD.` → `KNOW WHERE YOUR ROOTS ARE.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter twenty-nine, on constancy. It opens with a short, dense claim. The good, Epictetus says, is a certain state of the will, and so is the bad. Everything outside the will, money, health, reputation, even the body, is material the will works with. Earlier in the Discourses he puts it this way: as wood is the carpenter's material, each person's own life is the material of the art of living. The carpenter isn't good because the wood is fine, but because of what he does with it. That's where the roots are. If your good lives in your will, pressure on everything else is weather in the branches. A threat to your job, your comfort, your standing: those are leaves, real and worth caring about, but not the roots. Then Epictetus imagines the test. Someone powerful threatens you. Don't panic, he says; ask what is being threatened. If it's the body or the property, the will is still standing. He even pictures God calling a student forward as a witness: come and testify for me. Is anything outside the will good or bad? Will you show up and say it, or tremble and say the opposite? Constancy isn't stiffness, or refusing to feel the wind. It's knowing which part of you is supposed to move and which isn't. The week in a breath: never alone, blind, not wicked, a clay lamp, not my judgment, test the coin, a good opponent, and now stand firm.
screen: `THE GOOD IS A STATE OF THE WILL.` · `EVERYTHING ELSE IS MATERIAL.` · `CALLED FORWARD AS A WITNESS.` · `NOT STIFFNESS: KNOWING THE ROOTS.` · then, large: `STAND FIRM.`

segments.voice: Feel your feet flat on the floor, the ground solid under you. Let one pressure blow through like wind, a deadline, a hard conversation, someone's expectations, and notice what bends: plans, comfort, mood. Then come back to your feet, and to what doesn't need to bend: what you value, how you mean to act.
Stand firm. Epictetus' constancy: the good lives in the will, so let the branches move in the wind and keep the roots where they are.
Your line: let the branches move in the wind. The roots are yours. Day four hundred six, and the week is whole.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners prepare for pressure by naming in advance what could be lost and what couldn't, and anchoring themselves in their own choices.
